Writer’s guide

From question to historical argument

01

Choose

Select one prompt and one numbered position. You may refine the position, but your thesis must answer the prompt directly.

02

Research

Use the source map as a launch point. Build an argument from primary evidence and historical scholarship. Start with sources listed for your position, then read at least one source for a rival position so you can answer it as the Counter-Argument.

03

Cite

Cite the historical document, book, journal article, or original web publication - never this packet's page or a reader page as the source locator.

04

Flags

[IMAGE] marks a visual source. [RETROSPECTIVE] marks later testimony. [OUTSIDE DATES] marks evidence outside the prompt's focus range; use it only for context or comparison and identify the limitation.

Read the note on contested positions

Positions that need extra care. Every numbered position below can be defended, but these are thinly served or contested. Use the resolved reader guidance exactly as stated and do not cite a historian for a claim the historian does not make.

  • 8.2.2 · Thin; build it from the projects
    Why it is thin: Historians of early transportation stress mixed public-private enterprise. Few credit private capital alone, and even the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad drew city and state money.
    Closest in your readers: Dalzell (S8.05); Majewski (A8.45); Ward on railroad promotion (A8.60); Atack, Jaremski, and Rousseau on bank finance (A8.2).
    What you must do: Show which projects private investors actually financed, and treat state aid as the Counter-Argument rather than ignoring it.
  • 8.3.2 · Thinner than its rivals
    Why it is thin: Thomas Dublin, the leading historian of Lowell, ties the women’s protests to community and independence, so the strict exploitation reading has fewer book-length defenders.
    Closest in your readers: Dublin on the ten-hour movement (S8.08); Ginger (A8.24); Husband (A8.32); Vogel (A8.58).
    What you must do: Pair the scholarship with the women’s own words: the ten-hour petitions (S8.47) and the mill operatives’ writing in the Voice of Industry (S8.53).
  • 8.5.2 · Thin; argue from the evidence
    Why it is thin: No major historian argues that job competition was the main cause of 1850s nativism. Scholars treat it as one ingredient alongside religion and the collapse of the parties.
    Closest in your readers: Laurie (S8.14); Cohen (A8.13); Hammett (A8.27); Harris (A8.28).
    What you must do: Build the argument from findings (wage evidence, who the rioters were) and say plainly that you are doing so. Address religion as the Counter-Argument.
  • 9.1.3 · Thin as worded
    Why it is thin: No modern historian calls Marshall simply a Federalist partisan; most explicitly reject that reading. The charge belongs mainly to Marshall’s Jeffersonian critics, such as Spencer Roane and Jefferson himself.
    Closest in your readers: Stites on Federalist constitutionalism (S9.03); LaCroix (A9.29); Klarman (A9.26); Penick (A9.43).
    What you must do: Treat this position as the critics’ charge and test it. Quote the critics directly, and do not attribute the word “partisan” to a modern historian who does not use it.
  • 9.2.3 · Rests on a few works
    Why it is thin: The argument that one-party rule made politics personal and unaccountable rests on a small group of studies.
    Closest in your readers: Remini (S9.06); Wallace on changing ideas of party (A9.53); Mayo (A9.35); Skeen (A9.51).
    What you must do: Pair the scholarship with Martin Van Buren’s January 1827 letter to Thomas Ritchie (S9.66), the classic defense of party competition.
  • 9.4.3 · One main defender
    Why it is thin: Ernest May is essentially the only serious scholar who argues that the 1824 presidential rivalries shaped the doctrine. Most historians of the doctrine dispute him.
    Closest in your readers: May (S9.12) and May’s reply to Ammon (A9.34); Ammon’s critique (A9.2), to answer as the Counter-Argument.
    What you must do: Engage Ammon’s rebuttal directly, using John Quincy Adams’s November 1823 diary entries on the cabinet debates (S9.49, S9.59).
  • 10.2.1 · Thin in modern scholarship
    Why it is thin: No major modern historian makes the tariff the core of nullification. That reading survives in older tariff histories and in economists’ work.
    Closest in your readers: Freehling on South Carolina’s economic grievances (S10.04); Ochenkowski (A10.28); Capers (A10.9).
    What you must do: Build the case from the South Carolina Protest (S10.3) and the Ordinance of Nullification (S10.31), then answer Freehling’s slavery argument (S10.05) as the Counter-Argument.
  • 10.3.1 · Contested but defended
    Why it is thin: Paternalism has serious defenders, among them Francis Paul Prucha and Robert Remini, but recent scholarship (Saunt, Rogin, Cave) largely rejects it.
    Closest in your readers: Remini (S10.07); Shire on “sympathetic paternalism” as a qualified middle position (A10.43).
    What you must do: The position is defensible, but you must answer Saunt (S10.08) as the Counter-Argument. The phrase “sincerely if wrongly” in the position already signals this.
  • 11.1.2 · Contested but defended
    Why it is thin: Eugene Genovese’s pre-capitalist reading is now a minority view after the new history of capitalism, but it remains a major interpretive tradition.
    Closest in your readers: Genovese (S11.02); Egerton, “Markets without a Market Revolution” (A8.20).
    What you must do: Name the Genovese tradition, and answer Walter Johnson (S11.01) or Baptist as the Counter-Argument.
  • 12.4.2 · Narrower than its rivals
    Why it is thin: Fewer works make church work and benevolence, rather than abolition, the main root of the women’s rights movement.
    Closest in your readers: Ryan (S12.11); Boylan (A12.3, A12.4); Ryan on women’s networks (A12.41).
    What you must do: Be careful with Nancy Hewitt (A12.25): her work supports 12.4.1 more than 12.4.2. Engage the Declaration of Sentiments (S12.46) directly.
  • 12.5.2 · A minority position; defensible
    Why it is thin: Recent historians emphasize the transcendentalists’ reform work. The individualism critique comes mainly from literary and cultural critics.
    Closest in your readers: Gura on self-reliance (S12.14); Goodman’s encyclopedia entries (W12.14, W12.15).
    What you must do: Label this a critics’ tradition, use Emerson’s “Self-Reliance” (S12.35) as evidence, and answer Gougeon (A12.20) as the Counter-Argument.

Chapter 8 · 1793–1854

8.1 · Revolution or Evolution?

Was the transformation of the American economy between 1815 and 1850 a genuine revolution that broke with an older way of life, or the speeding-up of commercial habits Americans already had?

E Pluribus Unum · Unit 3 · An Expanding Nation

Was the transformation of the American economy between 1815 and 1850 a genuine revolution that broke with an older way of life, or the speeding-up of commercial habits Americans already had?

Choose and defend one of the following positions:

  1. 8.1.1 A market revolution: the spread of markets, wage work, and credit overturned a household-centered, neighborly rural economy and forced Americans into a new capitalist order.
  2. 8.1.2 An evolution: rural Americans were already buying, selling, and borrowing for distant markets before 1815; the new roads, canals, and railroads accelerated habits that were already there.
  3. 8.1.3 A communications and transportation revolution: the real break was in how fast goods, people, and information moved, and that, more than any change in values, remade American life.
Keep in focus: 1815-1850. Stay within this period, and name which interpretive tradition you are engaging rather than simply listing new inventions.
In Plain Terms

Question: Was the new economy a sharp break from the past or a gradual change?

  • 8.1.1 It was a sharp break: markets and wage work destroyed an older, more self-sufficient way of life.
  • 8.1.2 It was gradual: farmers were already selling to markets; the changes just sped things up.
  • 8.1.3 The biggest change was speed: faster travel and communication remade the country.

Chapter 8 · 1793–1854

8.2 · Who Built the Infrastructure?

Who deserves the most credit for the roads, canals, and railroads that knit the nation together before 1850?

E Pluribus Unum · Unit 3 · An Expanding Nation

Who deserves the most credit for the roads, canals, and railroads that knit the nation together before 1850?

Choose and defend one of the following positions:

  1. 8.2.1 State governments: states such as New York and Pennsylvania planned, financed, and owned the projects that mattered most, from the Erie Canal on.
  2. 8.2.2 Private enterprise: entrepreneurs, investors, and corporations took the risks and supplied the capital and know-how that built the transportation network.
  3. 8.2.3 The federal government: through the National Road, land grants, surveys, the postal system, and the Army Corps of Engineers, Washington played a larger role than its constitutional debates suggest.
Keep in focus: 1806-1850. Stay within these dates, and judge credit by who planned and paid for specific projects, not only by who argued about them.
In Plain Terms

Question: Who did the most to build America's roads, canals, and railroads?

  • 8.2.1 State governments did, by planning and paying for big projects like the Erie Canal.
  • 8.2.2 Private businesses and investors did, by risking their own money.
  • 8.2.3 The national government did more than people think, through roads, land grants, and engineers.

Chapter 8 · 1793–1854

8.3 · The Mill Girls of Lowell

For the young women who worked in the Lowell textile mills, was factory work chiefly a path to independence, a new form of exploitation, or a system of moral supervision designed by the owners?

E Pluribus Unum · Unit 3 · An Expanding Nation

For the young women who worked in the Lowell textile mills, was factory work chiefly a path to independence, a new form of exploitation, or a system of moral supervision designed by the owners?

Choose and defend one of the following positions:

  1. 8.3.1 A path to independence: wages, shared boardinghouse life, and distance from home gave mill women unprecedented personal and economic independence and a sense of sisterhood.
  2. 8.3.2 A new form of exploitation: speed-ups, wage cuts, and long hours turned mill work into "wage slavery" and provoked the women's strikes and petitions of the 1830s and 1840s.
  3. 8.3.3 A system of paternalist control: the Boston Associates designed boardinghouses, curfews, and church rules to keep a respectable, docile workforce and avoid the English factory towns.
Keep in focus: 1823-1850. Stay within the Lowell system and its workers; use the women's own words wherever you can.
In Plain Terms

Question: Was working in the Lowell mills good or bad for young women?

  • 8.3.1 Good: it gave them their own money, friends, and freedom.
  • 8.3.2 Bad: owners cut wages and sped up work, so the women protested.
  • 8.3.3 It was about control: the owners built the whole system to keep the workers in line.

Chapter 8 · 1793–1854

8.4 · Did Workers Become a Class?

As wage labor replaced the artisan workshop, did American workers develop a shared class consciousness, or did other loyalties divide them?

E Pluribus Unum · Unit 3 · An Expanding Nation

As wage labor replaced the artisan workshop, did American workers develop a shared class consciousness, or did other loyalties divide them?

Choose and defend one of the following positions:

  1. 8.4.1 Yes, through artisan republicanism: workers drew on Revolutionary ideals of independence and equality to build unions, workingmen's parties, and a real working-class movement.
  2. 8.4.2 No, because religion and middle-class reform pulled workers toward employers: revivals, temperance, and the ideal of self-improvement blunted class conflict.
  3. 8.4.3 No, because race, ethnicity, and religion fractured workers: native-born Protestants, Irish Catholics, and Black workers rarely saw themselves as one class, and "whiteness" often mattered more than wages.
Keep in focus: 1820-1850. Stay within this period, and engage what workers actually did (strikes, unions, parties, riots), not only what reformers said about them.
In Plain Terms

Question: Did workers come to see themselves as one united group?

  • 8.4.1 Yes: they used the ideals of the Revolution to organize unions and parties.
  • 8.4.2 No: religion and reform made many workers side with their bosses.
  • 8.4.3 No: differences of race, ethnicity, and religion kept workers divided.

Chapter 8 · 1793–1854

8.5 · The Roots of Nativism

What best explains the surge of anti-immigrant nativism that culminated in the Know-Nothing movement of the 1850s?

E Pluribus Unum · Unit 3 · An Expanding Nation

What best explains the surge of anti-immigrant nativism that culminated in the Know-Nothing movement of the 1850s?

Choose and defend one of the following positions:

  1. 8.5.1 Religious prejudice: nativism was above all a Protestant crusade against Catholicism and the supposed power of the pope.
  2. 8.5.2 Economic competition: native-born workers blamed cheap Irish and German labor for falling wages and lost jobs.
  3. 8.5.3 Political crisis: the Know-Nothings rose because the Whig-Democratic party system was collapsing under the slavery issue, and nativism offered voters a new home.
Keep in focus: 1830-1856. Stay within these dates, and explain the movement's timing, not only its prejudices.
In Plain Terms

Question: Why did so many Americans turn against immigrants?

  • 8.5.1 Mainly religion: Protestants feared and hated Catholics.
  • 8.5.2 Mainly jobs: workers thought immigrants were taking their work and lowering pay.
  • 8.5.3 Mainly politics: the old parties were falling apart over slavery, and nativism filled the gap.

Chapter 9 · 1811–1828

9.1 · The Marshall Court

What was the Marshall Court's most important purpose in decisions such as Dartmouth College v. Woodward, McCulloch v. Maryland, and Gibbons v. Ogden?

E Pluribus Unum · Unit 3 · An Expanding Nation

What was the Marshall Court's most important purpose in decisions such as Dartmouth College v. Woodward, McCulloch v. Maryland, and Gibbons v. Ogden?

Choose and defend one of the following positions:

  1. 9.1.1 Building the nation: Marshall used the Court to establish federal supremacy and a lasting constitutional union.
  2. 9.1.2 Protecting property and enterprise: the Court's real achievement was securing contracts, corporations, and a national market for capitalism.
  3. 9.1.3 Continuing Federalist politics by other means: with the Federalist Party dying, Marshall wrote its program into constitutional law over the objections of Jeffersonian Republicans.
Keep in focus: 1810-1824. Stay within these decisions and the reactions to them; engage the arguments of the opinions and their critics, not just the outcomes.
In Plain Terms

Question: What was the Supreme Court under John Marshall really trying to do?

  • 9.1.1 Make the national government strong and keep the Union together.
  • 9.1.2 Protect business, property, and contracts.
  • 9.1.3 Keep the old Federalist Party's ideas alive through court decisions.

Chapter 9 · 1811–1828

9.2 · An Era of Good Feelings?

How accurate is the label "Era of Good Feelings" for the years of James Monroe's presidency?

E Pluribus Unum · Unit 3 · An Expanding Nation

How accurate is the label "Era of Good Feelings" for the years of James Monroe's presidency?

Choose and defend one of the following positions:

  1. 9.2.1 Largely accurate: the War of 1812 produced a genuine national consensus on banking, tariffs, and internal improvements, and partisan warfare faded.
  2. 9.2.2 A façade: beneath one-party rule, the Panic of 1819 and the Missouri crisis exposed deep economic and sectional divisions.
  3. 9.2.3 Accurate but harmful: the absence of party competition left politics personal, factional, and unaccountable until a new two-party system emerged in the late 1820s.
Keep in focus: 1817-1825. Stay within Monroe's two terms, and test the label against specific events, not just its general tone.
In Plain Terms

Question: Were Monroe's years really an "Era of Good Feelings"?

  • 9.2.1 Yes: after the war, Americans mostly agreed and party fighting faded.
  • 9.2.2 No: the Panic of 1819 and the Missouri fight showed deep divisions.
  • 9.2.3 Yes, but it was bad for democracy: with only one party, politics became personal and unaccountable.

Chapter 9 · 1811–1828

9.3 · The Missouri Crisis

What was the Missouri crisis of 1819-1821 fundamentally about?

E Pluribus Unum · Unit 3 · An Expanding Nation

What was the Missouri crisis of 1819-1821 fundamentally about?

Choose and defend one of the following positions:

  1. 9.3.1 The morality and future of slavery: northern opponents of Missouri's admission were genuinely trying to stop slavery's spread, and southerners understood it that way.
  2. 9.3.2 Sectional political power: the fight was over control of Congress and the presidency, and the three-fifths clause mattered more than enslaved people's freedom.
  3. 9.3.3 The meaning of the Union and the Constitution: the deeper quarrel was over whether Congress could impose conditions on new states, which made the compromise as much a constitutional settlement as a moral one.
Keep in focus: 1819-1821. Stay within the congressional debates and public reactions; engage the actual arguments made, not only the compromise's terms.
In Plain Terms

Question: What was the fight over Missouri really about?

  • 9.3.1 Slavery itself: northerners wanted to stop it from spreading.
  • 9.3.2 Power: each section wanted control of Congress and the presidency.
  • 9.3.3 The Constitution: could Congress put conditions on new states?

Prompt 8 of 25
9

Chapter 9 · 1811–1828

9.4 · The Monroe Doctrine

What best explains the Monroe Doctrine of 1823?

E Pluribus Unum · Unit 3 · An Expanding Nation

What best explains the Monroe Doctrine of 1823?

Choose and defend one of the following positions:

  1. 9.4.1 Republican idealism: the United States was defending the independence of new Latin American republics against European monarchies.
  2. 9.4.2 National security and realism: Adams and Monroe were protecting U.S. interests against Russia, Spain, and the Holy Alliance, knowing the British navy would enforce the policy.
  3. 9.4.3 Domestic politics: the doctrine was shaped by the rivalries of men competing for the presidency in 1824.
  4. 9.4.4 The foundation of empire: the doctrine announced U.S. claims to dominance over the Western Hemisphere that later generations would act upon.
Keep in focus: 1817-1826. Stay within these dates; if you argue position 4, you must show what in 1823 already pointed toward hemispheric dominance rather than reading later history backward.
In Plain Terms

Question: Why did the United States issue the Monroe Doctrine?

  • 9.4.1 To support new republics in Latin America.
  • 9.4.2 To protect American safety and interests, counting on Britain's navy.
  • 9.4.3 Because of political competition among men who wanted to be president.
  • 9.4.4 To begin claiming power over the whole hemisphere.

Chapter 9 · 1811–1828

9.5 · Why Jackson Won in 1828

What best explains Andrew Jackson's victory in the election of 1828?

E Pluribus Unum · Unit 3 · An Expanding Nation

What best explains Andrew Jackson's victory in the election of 1828?

Choose and defend one of the following positions:

  1. 9.5.1 The rise of the common man: expanded white male suffrage and popular resentment of the "corrupt bargain" swept a hero of the people into office.
  2. 9.5.2 Party organization: Martin Van Buren and his allies built a new national coalition, with newspapers, committees, and patronage, that out-organized Adams.
  3. 9.5.3 Image and campaign technique: the first modern campaign sold Jackson's personal story, military fame, and persona more than any program.
Keep in focus: 1824-1828. Stay within the two elections, and use election evidence (campaign materials, results, letters) rather than Jackson's later presidency.
In Plain Terms

Question: Why did Andrew Jackson win the 1828 election?

  • 9.5.1 Ordinary men could now vote, and they were angry about the "corrupt bargain."
  • 9.5.2 Van Buren built a powerful party organization behind him.
  • 9.5.3 His campaign sold his image as a war hero and man of the people.

Prompt 10 of 25
10

Chapter 10 · 1828–1840

10.1 · How Democratic Was Jacksonian Democracy?

Did the political changes of the Jacksonian era expand democracy, or did they redefine it in ways that excluded as many Americans as they included?

E Pluribus Unum · Unit 3 · An Expanding Nation

Did the political changes of the Jacksonian era expand democracy, or did they redefine it in ways that excluded as many Americans as they included?

Choose and defend one of the following positions:

  1. 10.1.1 A real expansion: the end of property qualifications, popular party conventions, and mass voting made the United States the most democratic nation in the world.
  2. 10.1.2 A white man's democracy: rights for white men grew at the same time that free Black men lost the vote, women stayed excluded, and Native nations were removed.
  3. 10.1.3 A democracy of ambitious capitalists: Jacksonians wanted an equal chance to get rich, so their democracy opened markets and opportunity more than it challenged inequality.
Keep in focus: 1824-1840. Stay within this period, and weigh who gained and who lost political rights, not only how many votes were cast.
In Plain Terms

Question: Did democracy really grow during Jackson's era?

  • 10.1.1 Yes: far more ordinary men could vote and take part in politics.
  • 10.1.2 Only for white men: Black men, women, and Native peoples lost ground.
  • 10.1.3 It was mostly about letting more men compete to get rich.

Chapter 10 · 1828–1840

10.2 · The Nullification Crisis

What was really at stake in South Carolina's nullification crisis of 1832-1833?

E Pluribus Unum · Unit 3 · An Expanding Nation

What was really at stake in South Carolina's nullification crisis of 1832-1833?

Choose and defend one of the following positions:

  1. 10.2.1 The tariff: South Carolinians believed protective tariffs were ruining the cotton economy, and the crisis was about economic survival.
  2. 10.2.2 Slavery: nullifiers feared that a federal government able to impose tariffs could someday attack slavery, so they fought to establish a state veto first.
  3. 10.2.3 The nature of the Union: the core conflict was constitutional, between a compact of sovereign states and a perpetual national union.
Keep in focus: 1828-1833. Stay within these dates, and engage the arguments of Calhoun, Webster, Hayne, and Jackson themselves.
In Plain Terms

Question: What was the fight over nullification really about?

  • 10.2.1 Money: South Carolina thought tariffs were destroying its economy.
  • 10.2.2 Slavery: they wanted the power to block any future federal attack on slavery.
  • 10.2.3 The Constitution: was the Union a deal between states, or a permanent nation?

Chapter 10 · 1828–1840

10.3 · Explaining Indian Removal

What best explains the Indian Removal policy of the 1830s and the Trail of Tears?

E Pluribus Unum · Unit 3 · An Expanding Nation

What best explains the Indian Removal policy of the 1830s and the Trail of Tears?

Choose and defend one of the following positions:

  1. 10.3.1 Paternalism: Jackson and his allies believed, sincerely if wrongly, that removal west of the Mississippi was the only way to save Native peoples from destruction.
  2. 10.3.2 Land, cotton, and slavery: removal was a deliberate dispossession that cleared the way for white settlers, speculators, and the expansion of slave-based cotton plantations.
  3. 10.3.3 States' rights and federal power: removal grew out of Georgia's claim to sovereignty over Cherokee land and Jackson's refusal to enforce the Supreme Court against a state.
Keep in focus: 1829-1839. Stay within these dates, and include the voices and strategies of Native nations, not only the decisions made about them.
In Plain Terms

Question: Why did the government force Native peoples to move west?

  • 10.3.1 Leaders claimed, and some believed, that moving was the only way to save them.
  • 10.3.2 White Americans wanted the land for cotton farms worked by enslaved people.
  • 10.3.3 Georgia claimed power over Cherokee land, and Jackson backed the state over the Supreme Court.

Chapter 10 · 1828–1840

10.4 · The Bank War and the Panic of 1837

How responsible was Andrew Jackson's war on the Second Bank of the United States for the Panic of 1837 and the depression that followed?

E Pluribus Unum · Unit 3 · An Expanding Nation

How responsible was Andrew Jackson's war on the Second Bank of the United States for the Panic of 1837 and the depression that followed?

Choose and defend one of the following positions:

  1. 10.4.1 Largely responsible: destroying the Bank, moving deposits to "pet banks," and the Specie Circular unleashed speculation and then a crash.
  2. 10.4.2 Partly responsible but justified: the Bank War was a necessary defense of democracy against a concentrated "money power," whatever its economic costs.
  3. 10.4.3 Not chiefly responsible: the panic came from international forces, especially British credit tightening and shifts in silver flows and cotton prices, that Jackson did not control.
Keep in focus: 1832-1843. Stay within these dates, and separate whether the Bank War was wise politics from whether it caused the panic.
In Plain Terms

Question: Did Jackson's fight with the national bank cause the Panic of 1837?

  • 10.4.1 Yes: his attacks on the bank led to wild speculation and then a crash.
  • 10.4.2 Partly, but it was still the right thing to do to protect democracy from powerful bankers.
  • 10.4.3 No: the crash mostly came from problems overseas, especially in Britain.

Chapter 10 · 1828–1840

10.5 · Judging Jackson's Presidency

What should define Andrew Jackson's legacy as president?

E Pluribus Unum · Unit 3 · An Expanding Nation

What should define Andrew Jackson's legacy as president?

Choose and defend one of the following positions:

  1. 10.5.1 A strengthened democratic presidency and Union: Jackson made the presidency the voice of the people and defended the Union against nullification.
  2. 10.5.2 Executive overreach: as his Whig opponents charged, "King Andrew" abused the veto, defied the courts, and concentrated power in his own hands.
  3. 10.5.3 Racial exclusion: Jackson's legacy rests above all on Indian Removal and the defense of slavery, which defined whose nation the United States would be.
Keep in focus: 1829-1837. Stay within Jackson's two terms; you may use one later source only to show how his legacy was being judged.
In Plain Terms

Question: How should we remember Andrew Jackson as president?

  • 10.5.1 As a strong leader who spoke for ordinary people and saved the Union.
  • 10.5.2 As a power-hungry president who acted like a king, just as the Whigs said.
  • 10.5.3 Above all for removing Native peoples and protecting slavery.

Prompt 15 of 25
11

Chapter 11 · 1790–1860

11.1 · Slavery and Capitalism

Was the slave economy of the Cotton Kingdom a form of capitalism?

E Pluribus Unum · Unit 3 · An Expanding Nation

Was the slave economy of the Cotton Kingdom a form of capitalism?

Choose and defend one of the following positions:

  1. 11.1.1 Yes, slavery was central to American capitalism: cotton picked by enslaved people drove national and global growth, and enslavers used credit, markets, and accounting like modern businessmen.
  2. 11.1.2 No, the slave South was a distinct, pre-capitalist society: enslavers saw themselves as paternalist masters, not capitalists, and their world was organized around mastery rather than profit alone.
  3. 11.1.3 Profitable but self-limiting: slavery made enslavers rich, but it discouraged cities, immigration, manufacturing, and investment, leaving the South economically behind.
Keep in focus: 1800-1860. Stay within these dates, and support claims about the economy with evidence of how enslavers and markets actually operated.
In Plain Terms

Question: Was slavery in the cotton South a kind of capitalism?

  • 11.1.1 Yes: slave-grown cotton powered the whole American and world economy.
  • 11.1.2 No: enslavers saw themselves as fatherly masters, not businessmen.
  • 11.1.3 It made enslavers rich but kept the South from developing like the North.

Chapter 11 · 1790–1860

11.2 · Why Non-Enslavers Supported Slavery

Why did most white southerners who owned no enslaved people support slavery and its expansion?

E Pluribus Unum · Unit 3 · An Expanding Nation

Why did most white southerners who owned no enslaved people support slavery and its expansion?

Choose and defend one of the following positions:

  1. 11.2.1 Racial solidarity: slavery guaranteed every white man a status above Black people, whatever his wealth.
  2. 11.2.2 Economic ties and ambition: many yeomen hired enslaved labor, sold to planters, were kin to enslavers, or hoped to become enslavers themselves.
  3. 11.2.3 Household mastery: yeoman farmers defended slavery because it protected a patriarchal order in which they, too, were masters of their own households.
  4. 11.2.4 Planter dominance: support was less freely given than it looked, because planters controlled politics, the press, and law, and silenced poor-white dissent.
Keep in focus: 1820-1860. Stay within these dates, and use evidence from or about non-enslaving whites themselves, not only from planters.
In Plain Terms

Question: Why did white southerners who did not own slaves still support slavery?

  • 11.2.1 Because slavery made every white man feel superior to Black people.
  • 11.2.2 Because they made money from it or hoped to own slaves one day.
  • 11.2.3 Because it protected their power as heads of their own families.
  • 11.2.4 Because rich planters controlled the South and silenced those who disagreed.

How should historians best describe the relationship between enslavers and enslaved people in the antebellum South?

Choose and defend one of the following positions:

  1. 11.3.1 Paternalism: enslavers claimed a fatherly duty toward enslaved people, and enslaved people used those claims to win limited protections, creating a relationship of mutual obligations.
  2. 11.3.2 Commodification and violence: the domestic slave trade, the whip, and the pushing system made enslaved people above all property to be bought, sold, and driven for profit.
  3. 11.3.3 Negotiation and struggle: the terms of slavery were constantly contested, shifting with region, crop, and time as enslaved people pushed back against enslavers' demands.
Keep in focus: 1808-1860. Stay within these dates, and include testimony from enslaved people themselves, noting when an account was recorded long after the events.
In Plain Terms

Question: What was the relationship between enslavers and enslaved people really like?

  • 11.3.1 Enslavers claimed to be fatherly protectors, and enslaved people used that claim to get small protections.
  • 11.3.2 Enslaved people were treated as property to be sold and forced to work through violence.
  • 11.3.3 It was a constant struggle, with enslaved people fighting over the terms of their lives.

Chapter 11 · 1790–1860

11.4 · Forms of Resistance

Which form of resistance did the most to defend enslaved people's humanity and challenge slavery?

E Pluribus Unum · Unit 3 · An Expanding Nation

Which form of resistance did the most to defend enslaved people's humanity and challenge slavery?

Choose and defend one of the following positions:

  1. 11.4.1 Armed revolt: rebellions such as Gabriel's, the German Coast Uprising, Denmark Vesey's conspiracy, and Nat Turner's showed that enslaved people would fight, and terrified enslavers.
  2. 11.4.2 Everyday resistance and flight: slowdowns, sabotage, truancy, and escape were far more common and steadily undermined enslavers' control.
  3. 11.4.3 Community, family, and faith: building families, African American Christianity, and song preserved identity and hope that slavery tried to destroy.
Keep in focus: 1800-1860. Stay within these dates, and define "resistance" clearly before you measure which form mattered most.
In Plain Terms

Question: Which kind of resistance mattered most for enslaved people?

  • 11.4.1 Armed rebellions, which showed enslaved people would fight back.
  • 11.4.2 Everyday acts like slowing down work or running away.
  • 11.4.3 Building families, faith, and community that slavery could not destroy.

Prompt 19 of 25
11

Chapter 11 · 1790–1860

11.5 · The Plantation Mistress

Were white plantation mistresses chiefly victims of southern patriarchy or active participants in slavery?

E Pluribus Unum · Unit 3 · An Expanding Nation

Were white plantation mistresses chiefly victims of southern patriarchy or active participants in slavery?

Choose and defend one of the following positions:

  1. 11.5.1 Victims of patriarchy: confined by their husbands' authority and humiliated by their sexual exploitation of enslaved women, many mistresses privately resented slavery.
  2. 11.5.2 Active enslavers: white women owned, bought, sold, managed, and violently disciplined enslaved people and profited from slavery in their own right.
  3. 11.5.3 Bound by race and class: whatever their grievances, mistresses identified with the slaveholding household and its racial order, which made real alliance with enslaved women impossible.
Keep in focus: 1820-1860. Stay within these dates, and test each position against what women did, not only what they wrote in diaries.
In Plain Terms

Question: Were plantation wives mostly victims or mostly enslavers?

  • 11.5.1 Victims: their husbands controlled them, and some quietly hated slavery.
  • 11.5.2 Enslavers: they owned, sold, and punished enslaved people themselves.
  • 11.5.3 Both, but their race and class kept them loyal to slavery.

Chapter 12 · 1825–1854

12.1 · The Second Great Awakening

What best explains the explosive growth of evangelical religion during the Second Great Awakening?

E Pluribus Unum · Unit 3 · An Expanding Nation

What best explains the explosive growth of evangelical religion during the Second Great Awakening?

Choose and defend one of the following positions:

  1. 12.1.1 The democratization of Christianity: ordinary believers and popular preachers rejected learned clergy and built churches in their own image, matching the democratic spirit of the age.
  2. 12.1.2 A response to the market revolution: revivals gave anxious Americans, especially the new middle class, discipline and order in a rapidly changing economy.
  3. 12.1.3 Women's leadership: women made up most converts and built the prayer meetings, networks, and benevolent societies that carried the revivals.
Keep in focus: 1800-1840. Stay within these dates, and explain why the revivals spread, not only what revivalists believed.
In Plain Terms

Question: Why did evangelical religion grow so fast in the early 1800s?

  • 12.1.1 Ordinary people took control of religion, just as they were taking control of politics.
  • 12.1.2 People in a fast-changing economy used religion to find order and self-control.
  • 12.1.3 Women led and spread the revivals.

Chapter 12 · 1825–1854

12.2 · Why Reform?

What motivated the reform movements of the 1820s-1850s, including temperance, asylums and prisons, public schools, and utopian communities?

E Pluribus Unum · Unit 3 · An Expanding Nation

What motivated the reform movements of the 1820s-1850s, including temperance, asylums and prisons, public schools, and utopian communities?

Choose and defend one of the following positions:

  1. 12.2.1 Religious perfectionism and humanitarianism: reformers believed people and society could be perfected and acted from genuine compassion and faith.
  2. 12.2.2 Social control: middle-class reformers sought to discipline workers, immigrants, and the poor and to impose order on a disorderly society.
  3. 12.2.3 Adjustment to the market economy: reform taught the self-discipline, sobriety, and punctuality a wage-earning, commercial society required.
Keep in focus: 1825-1854. Stay within these dates, and compare at least two different reform movements rather than resting your case on one.
In Plain Terms

Question: Why did reformers try to change American society?

  • 12.2.1 They truly believed people could be made better and wanted to help.
  • 12.2.2 They wanted to control workers, immigrants, and the poor.
  • 12.2.3 They wanted to train people to fit the new economy.

Chapter 12 · 1825–1854

12.3 · Who Drove Abolitionism?

Who did the most to turn antislavery into a powerful national movement before 1854?

E Pluribus Unum · Unit 3 · An Expanding Nation

Who did the most to turn antislavery into a powerful national movement before 1854?

Choose and defend one of the following positions:

  1. 12.3.1 White evangelical immediatists: William Lloyd Garrison and revival-inspired reformers made slavery a sin to be ended now, not gradually.
  2. 12.3.2 Black abolitionists and the enslaved: Black writers, speakers, communities, and fugitives from slavery led the movement and kept it radical.
  3. 12.3.3 Political abolitionists: the Liberty Party and antislavery politicians turned moral protest into votes and laws, which moral suasion alone could not do.
Keep in focus: 1829-1854. Stay within these dates, and explain how antislavery changed over time, from gradualism and colonization to immediatism.
In Plain Terms

Question: Who did the most to build the anti-slavery movement?

  • 12.3.1 White religious reformers like Garrison, who demanded an immediate end to slavery.
  • 12.3.2 Black abolitionists and people escaping slavery, who led and kept pushing.
  • 12.3.3 Politicians and new parties that turned anti-slavery ideas into votes.

Chapter 12 · 1825–1854

12.4 · Abolition and Women's Rights

Where did the women's rights movement that met at Seneca Falls in 1848 come from?

E Pluribus Unum · Unit 3 · An Expanding Nation

Where did the women's rights movement that met at Seneca Falls in 1848 come from?

Choose and defend one of the following positions:

  1. 12.4.1 Abolitionism: women's work against slavery, and the attacks they faced for speaking publicly, taught them to see and fight their own subordination.
  2. 12.4.2 Evangelical benevolence and domestic ideals: church work, moral reform societies, and the belief in women's moral authority gave women organizations and confidence.
  3. 12.4.3 Two movements, not one: Black women's activism, rooted in free Black communities and churches, ran on its own track, and white women's rights leaders often left race out.
Keep in focus: 1830-1854. Stay within these dates, and engage both the Declaration of Sentiments and at least one source by a Black woman.
In Plain Terms

Question: What led to the women's rights movement and the Seneca Falls Convention?

  • 12.4.1 Working against slavery made women see their own lack of rights.
  • 12.4.2 Church and charity work gave women organizations and confidence.
  • 12.4.3 Black women built their own movement, which white leaders often ignored.

Chapter 12 · 1825–1854

12.5 · Transcendentalism

Was transcendentalism chiefly a movement for social reform, a retreat into individualism, or a declaration of American cultural independence?

E Pluribus Unum · Unit 3 · An Expanding Nation

Was transcendentalism chiefly a movement for social reform, a retreat into individualism, or a declaration of American cultural independence?

Choose and defend one of the following positions:

  1. 12.5.1 Social reform: transcendentalists such as Thoreau, Fuller, and the founders of Brook Farm pushed Americans toward abolition, women's rights, and resistance to unjust laws.
  2. 12.5.2 Individualism: transcendentalism taught self-reliance and inner experience, turning people away from collective reform and institutions.
  3. 12.5.3 Cultural independence: its greatest achievement was declaring that America needed its own literature, philosophy, and identity rather than Europe's.
Keep in focus: 1830-1854. Stay within these dates, and engage what transcendentalists wrote and did, not only their later reputations.
In Plain Terms

Question: What was transcendentalism really about?

  • 12.5.1 Changing society by fighting slavery and unjust laws.
  • 12.5.2 Looking inward and relying on yourself instead of groups or institutions.
  • 12.5.3 Creating a truly American way of thinking and writing.
